bib.title: Chapter 1: Statistical thinking for programmers (Think Stats)

question: How can programming skill be used to turn data into knowledge, illustrated by whether first babies arrive late?
contributions: Contrasts anecdotal evidence with a statistical approach (data collection, descriptive statistics, EDA, hypothesis testing, estimation)
Introduces the NSFG Cycle 6 survey design and its record/table/field structure
Defines apparent effect, statistical significance and artifact

limits: Chapter is motivation and set-up; it reports no analysis result, only an expected ~13 hour difference left to the reader's exercise
NSFG is deliberately oversampled (Hispanics, African-Americans, teenagers), so population conclusions need weights (finalwgt); deferred to later chapters
Code is Python 2 (print statement) and relies on the author's survey.py and thinkstats.com URLs, which may have dated
No sources given for the 13 hours figure beyond the exercise
practices: Prefer data from a well-designed study over anecdotes, which suffer small samples, selection bias, confirmation bias and inaccuracy (Sec 1.1)
Use recodes unless there is a compelling reason to process raw data (Sec 1.4)
Check a new dataset by counting records and partitioning groups against the codebook to catch data errors and bugs (Ex 1.3)
Compare more than means (median, variance), ask if the effect could be chance, and whether it is an artifact of bias (Sec 1.5)
Check published answers for flaws in data or analysis and seek raw data (Sec 1.5)

terms.definition: Evidence, often personal, that is collected casually rather than by a well-designed study.
A group we are interested in studying, often a group of people, but the term is also used for animals, vegetables and minerals.
A study that collects data about a population at a particular point in time.
A study that follows a population over time, collecting data from the same group repeatedly.
A person who responds to a survey.
The subset of a population used to collect data.
A sample is representative if every member of the population has the same chance of being in the sample.
The technique of increasing the representation of a sub-population in order to avoid errors due to small sample sizes.
In a database, a collection of information about a single person or other object of study.
In a database, one of the named variables that makes up a record.
In a database, a collection of records.
Values collected and recorded with little or no checking, calculation or interpretation.
A value that is generated by calculation and other logic applied to raw data.
The result of a computation that reduces a dataset to a single number (or at least a smaller set of numbers) that captures some characteristic of the data.
A measurement or summary statistic that suggests that something interesting is happening.
An apparent effect is statistically significant if it is unlikely to occur by chance.
An apparent effect that is caused by bias, measurement error, or some other kind of error.
